frames.narration: Alice opens the mail app, which has no session for her. It redirects her browser to the identity provider with its client id, a return address, a state value, a nonce and a PKCE challenge.
She types her password once. The provider creates a single sign-on session, sets a secure cookie on its own domain, and sends her back to the mail app with a single-use authorization code.

The mail app's back end swaps the code for tokens. The provider signs an ID token with key k1, valid for 10 minutes, naming Alice, the audience mail, and authentication level 1. The mail app checks it using the public key it fetched earlier, and no call to the provider is needed for later requests.

Alice opens the payroll app. It redirects to the provider, which finds the session cookie and sends her straight back with a new code, with no prompt. The payroll app gets its own token with the audience payroll.
She tries to change a bank account. Payroll requires multi-factor proof from the last 5 minutes, but her token says level 1, so the app redirects back to the provider asking for level 2.
Alice approves with her passkey. The provider upgrades the same session to level 2, records the time, and issues a fresh payroll token. The mail app is not affected.

That night the provider rotates the signing key. It publishes k2 and signs new tokens with it, while k1 stays in the key set for another 10 minutes, so tokens already issued still verify. The apps refetch the set when they meet an unknown key id.

messages.label: publish k2, keep k1 for 10 min

frames.narration: Next morning Alice logs out. The provider ends session s-1 and puts two logout messages on the queue, one for each app that got a token for it.

Workers post each logout token to the app's back-channel address. Each app ends its local session and remembers s-1 as revoked, so even a token with minutes left no longer works. If an app were down, the message would be retried with growing delays.
